newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Tiny Swaziland warns South Africa over sugar.
newsitem.headline: Tiny Swaziland warns South Africa over sugar.

text.p: Caught in a sugar trade war with South Africa, Swaziland is pondering retaliation and will only rejoin talks to end the dispute if its neighbour restores help currently denied the tiny mountain kingdom.
The South African Sugar Association (SASA) announced in August it would cut Swaziland off from using the export terminal in the Indian Ocean port of Durban.
South Africa also refused Swazi access to research and training facilities, claiming that imports of cheaper Swazi sugar cost the local industry up to 275 million rand ($58.14 million) a year.
Swaziland benefited from duty-free access to South Africa through membership of the South African Customs Union (SACU).

The Swaziland Sugar Association claims the neighbours have the wrong people in their sights. It says its policy was not to sell sugar directly into the huge South African market and blames rogue traders for the sales.
But the Swazis, fearing losses from their biggest industry and foreign exchange earner, threatened to change their policy if there was no movement by the South Africans.
"A year down the line, we may have to sell sugar (in South Africa)," Swazi association president Brian Glassock told reporters.

The South African industry dwarfs that of Swaziland and expects a bumper crop of almost 2.4 million tonnes this year (April to March). The kingdom expects around 460,000 tonnes of sugar during its production year.

South Africa will have around a million tonnes of sugar for export. Swaziland expects to send around 200,000 tonnes to the United States and European Union under preferential sugar quotas at prices of up to three times the prevailing world market price.
The country will further export 30,000 tonnes to neighbouring Mozambique while the remaining 230,000 tonnes would go to domestic consumers and manufacturers.

"The crux of the matter is that the South Africans believe we sell sugar to South Africa and our sugar is cheaper compared to their sugar," said Themba Dlamini, managing director of Tibiyo Taka Ngwane -- the biggest stakeholder in the Swazi sugar industry.
Tibiyo, a company set up in the name of the Swazi nation, controls about 50 percent of the industry with the rest under the Commonwealth Development Corporation and foreign companies.
Obed Dlamini, Swazi sugar association chairman and a former prime minister, says political intervention is needed by Pretoria.
"We feel it has to be addressed politically," Dlamini told Reuters, adding that President Nelson Mandela had committed his country to free trade with its neighbours.
"We see a reversal of what the president has said being perpetuated by the South African Sugar Association."
Talks with South Africa's Department of Trade and Industry were inconclusive, Swazi officials said.
But they said all is not lost for the Swazi industry because exports were still being shipped from Maputo in Mozambique -- which had turned out to be nearer and cheaper for the industry.
Swaziland hoped for a solution and would only return to talks to end the dispute if research, training and export facilities were restored, Glassock said.
Tibiyo managing director Dlamini issued a warning.
"I'm not sure there is going to be a winner in the end. This obviously leads us to a price war," he said.
